headline: Nehru Nagar leads stations that breached safe limit of ground-level ozone this summer
text: New Delhi: Nehru Nagar was the most polluted with ground-level ozone this summer, with its monitoring station, located near Lajpat Nagar, exceeding the safe limit on 56 out of 61 days in April and May. Many other stations across the city have also exceeded the standard ozone level this summer, according to a latest report compiled by Delhi Pollution Control Committee ( DPCC ) in these two months. The report has been submitted to National Green Tribunal (NGT), which had taken suo motu cognisance of a TOI report, ‘Oh-zone! Why this prominent pollutant in Delhi air is becoming a cause for concern', dated April 24 on high ozone levels in Delhi. NGT had asked DPCC and Commission for Air Quality Management to submit a report on the steps being taken to reduce the impact of this gaseous pollutant. Ozone is produced from the complex interaction between nitrogen oxides and volatile organic compounds, which are emitted from vehicles, power plants, factories and other combustion sources. They undergo cyclic reactions in the presence of sunlight to generate ground-level ozone. DPCC stated Patparganj and Aurobindo Marg had witnessed ozone levels exceeding for 45 and 38 days, respectively. Ozone exceeded the safe limit for 29 days at Alipur, 32 days at Dr Karni Singh Shooting Range, 25 days at Mandir Marg, and 20 days at RK Puram. However, the average ozone concentration in April and May was the highest at 224.9 micrograms per cubic metre at Nehru Nagar against the standard of 100 micrograms per cubic metre. This was followed by Patparganj and RK Puram recording 188.3 and 175.4 micrograms per cubic metre, respectively. "Central Pollution Control Board's data shows that Nehru Nagar, Dr Karni Singh Shooting Range, Jawaharlal Stadium, Major Dhyan Chand National Stadium, Nehru Nagar and RK Puram saw high ozone levels, which were more than the national ambient air quality standard of 100 micrograms per cubic metre for eight hours. The ozone levels were at peak during 11am to 6pm," said DPCC's report. Ground-level ozone, a highly reactive gas, has serious health consequences. "Those with respiratory conditions, asthma and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease — as well as children with premature lungs and older adults — are at serious risk. This can inflame and damage airways, make lungs susceptible to infection, aggravate asthma, emphysema and chronic bronchitis, and increase the frequency of asthma attacks leading to increased hospitalisation," said a report by Centre for Science and Environment.

In many ways, it reflects a broader cultural shift — from a community rooted in refugee resilience to a dynamic academic microcosm that symbolises aspiration and diversity.
